claims.claim: Raji cells contain 50–60 EBV episomes, allowing an easy detection of ORC/MCM at oriP.
claims.source: Raji cells contain 50–60 EBV episomes, allowing an easy detection of ORC/MCM at oriP (Adams et al., 1973).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claims.claim: The viral protein EBNA1 recruits ORC to oriP's dyad symmetry element, followed by MCM-DH loading.
claims.source: The viral protein EBNA1 recruits ORC to oriP's dyad symmetry element, followed by MCM-DH loading.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about EBV replication.

claims.claim: Both ORC and MCM were detected at the dyad symmetry element in G1, whereas a population containing S-G2-M-phased cells depicted a reduction in MCM levels.
claims.source: We detected both ORC and MCM at the dyad symmetry element in G1, whereas a population containing S-G2-M-phased cells depict a reduction in MCM levels, as expected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c; Papior et al., 2012; Ritzi et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in the referenced figure and supported by cited studies.

claims.claim: ChIP-seq of two replicates for ORC subunits (Orc2, Orc3) and of three replicates for MCM proteins (Mcm3, Mcm7) resulted in reproducible, but dispersed, ChIP-seq signals.
claims.source: ChIP-seq of two replicates for ORC subunits (Orc2, Orc3) and of three replicates for MCM proteins (Mcm3, Mcm7) resulted in reproducible, but dispersed, ChIP-seq signals as exemplified by the well-characterized replication origin Mcm4/PRKDC (Figure 1a; Ladenburger et al., 2002; Schaarschmidt et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the ChIP-seq profiles shown in Figure 1a.

claims.claim: The input control was significantly underrepresented in DNase hypersensitive (HS) regions, at TSSs, and at early RTDs.
claims.source: In line with a previous report (Teytelman et al., 2009), the input control was significantly underrepresented in DNase hypersensitive (HS) regions, at TSSs, and at early RTDs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b–d).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in the referenced figure and supported by a cited study.

claims.claim: Sonication-hypersensitive regions correlate with DNase HS regions.
claims.source: As sonication-hypersensitive regions correlate with DNase HS regions (Schwartz et al., 2005), we carefully compared our results obtained with and without input normalization.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claims.claim: The Pearson correlation coefficient of the relative read frequencies of Orc2/Orc3 is r = 0.866.
claims.source: The reliability and reproducibility of our ChIP experiments is reflected by the high Pearson correlation coefficients of the relative read frequencies of Orc2/Orc3 (r = 0.866, Figure 1c) and Mcm3/Mcm7 (r = 0.879, Figure 1d).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the correlation plot shown in Figure 1c.

claims.claim: The Pearson correlation coefficient of the relative read frequencies of Mcm3/Mcm7 is r = 0.879.
claims.source: The reliability and reproducibility of our ChIP experiments is reflected by the high Pearson correlation coefficients of the relative read frequencies of Orc2/Orc3 (r = 0.866, Figure 1c) and Mcm3/Mcm7 (r = 0.879, Figure 1d).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the correlation plot shown in Figure 1d.

claims.claim: ORC ChIP-seq data shows substantial enrichment around K562 Orc2 peaks.
claims.source: To compare our ChIP-seq data to previously published Orc2 ChIP-seq from asynchronously cycling K562 cells (GSE70165; Miotto et al., 2016), we calculated the relative read frequencies of our ORC ChIPs around an aggregate of K562 Orc2 peaks (>1 kb) and found substantial enrichment (Figure 1—figure supplement 3e).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claims.claim: Orc2 co-localizes with DNase HS sites present at active promoters and enhancers.
claims.source: Miotto et al., 2016 reported that Orc2 co-localizes with DNase HS sites present at active promoters and enhancers.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claims.claim: There is a significant enrichment of ORC at DNase HS regions > 1 kb, compared to regions deprived of DNase HS sites.
claims.source: In line with these observations, we found a significant enrichment of ORC at DNase HS regions > 1 kb, compared to regions deprived of DNase HS sites, with or without input normalization (Figure 1—figure supplement 3f, g).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: 2957 ascending segments (ASs) with an average size of 52.3 kb were selected, covering 4.9% (155 Mb) of the genome.
claims.source: In total, we selected 2957 ASs, with an average size of 52.3 kb, which covered 4.9% (155 Mb) of the genome (Figure 2a, green bars, Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the OK-seq analysis and summarized in Table 1.

claims.claim: 2451 (83%) of all AS located close to genic regions.
claims.source: In total, 2451 (83%) of all AS located close to genic regions (ASs extended by 20 kb on both sides overlapped with at least one annotated gene).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of AS positions relative to annotated genes.

claims.claim: 673 ASs (22.8% of all ASs) were flanked by actively transcribed genes on both sides (type 1 AS).
claims.source: Performing RNA-seq in asynchronously cycling Raji cells, we determined that 673 ASs (22.8% of all ASs) were flanked by actively transcribed genes (transcripts per kilobase per million [TPM] >3) on both sides (type 1 AS), with less than 20 kb between AS borders and the closest transcribed gene.
claims.evidence: This is based on combined analysis of OK-seq and RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: 1026 ASs (34.7%) had only one border associated to a transcribed gene (type 2 AS).
claims.source: In total, 1026 ASs (34.7%) had only one border associated to a transcribed gene (type 2 AS; TPM >3).
claims.evidence: This is based on combined analysis of OK-seq and RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: 506 ASs (17.1%) were devoid of proximal genes (non-genic AS).
claims.source: Also, 506 ASs (17.1%) were devoid of proximal genes (non-genic AS) (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on combined analysis of OK-seq and gene annotation data.

claims.claim: Type 1 ASs were on average slightly more efficient than type 2 ASs, followed by non-genic ASs.
claims.source: The slope did not change considerably between the different AS types, although type 1 ASs were on average slightly more efficient, followed by type 2 ASs, then non-genic ASs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of RFD slopes shown in the referenced figure.

claims.claim: Type 1 and 2 ASs located within early RTDs, while non-genic ASs were predominantly late replicating.
claims.source: Type 1 and 2 ASs located within early RTDs, while non-genic ASs were predominantly late replicating (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), as previously observed in GM06990 and HeLa (Petryk et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis shown in the referenced figure and supported by a cited study.

claims.claim: Both ORC and MCM were, on average, enriched within ASs compared to flanking regions.
claims.source: Both ORC and MCM were, on average, enriched within ASs compared to flanking regions (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a without input division).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the aggregate analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: Transcriptional activity in AS flanking regions was associated with increased ORC/MCM levels inside ASs and a prominent MCM depletion from transcribed regions.
claims.source: Transcriptional activity in AS flanking regions was associated with increased ORC/MCM levels inside ASs (compare Figure 2b, c) and a prominent MCM depletion from transcribed regions (Figure 2c, d, right border).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of different AS types shown in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: In type 2 ASs, ORC/MCM levels remained elevated at non-transcribed AS borders.
claims.source: In contrast, in type 2 ASs, ORC/MCM levels remained elevated at non-transcribed AS borders (Figure 2d, left border).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 2d.

claims.claim: No ORC/MCM enrichment was detected within non-genic ASs.
claims.source: No ORC/MCM enrichment was detected within non-genic ASs (Figure 2e).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 2e.

claims.claim: AS borders associated with transcriptional activity were locally enriched in ORC/MCM.
claims.source: AS borders associated with transcriptional activity were locally enriched in ORC/MCM (Figure 2c, d, both and right borders respectively).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figures 2c and 2d.

claims.claim: Orc1 accumulation at AS borders was previously detected.
claims.source: This is in line with previously detected Orc1 accumulation at AS borders (Petryk et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claims.claim: Non-genic AS borders only showed a local dip in ORC/MCM levels.
claims.source: Reciprocally, non-genic AS borders only showed a local dip in ORC/MCM levels (Figure 2d, left border; Figure 2e, both borders), but the biological significance of this observation remains unclear.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: The average RFD profile of active genes revealed strong ASs upstream of TSSs and downstream of transcriptional termination site (TTSs), and descending RFD segments (DSs) across the active gene bodies.
claims.source: Consistent with previous OK-seq studies (Chen et al., 2019; Petryk et al., 2016), the average RFD profile of active genes revealed strong ASs upstream of TSSs and downstream of transcriptional termination site (TTSs), and descending RFD segments (DSs) across the active gene bodies (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figure and supported by cited studies.

claims.claim: Silent genes displayed an overall flat RFD profile.
claims.source: This behavior depended on transcriptional activity as silent genes displayed an overall flat RFD profile (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claims.claim: The ORC relative read distribution was significantly enriched at active TSSs.
claims.source: When setting our ORC/MCM ChIP-seq data in relation to transcription, we observed that the ORC relative read distribution was significantly enriched at active TSSs, as already demonstrated in Drosophila (MacAlpine et al., 2010) and human cells (Dellino et al., 2013; Miotto et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the ChIP-seq analysis and supported by cited studies.

claims.claim: ORC relative read distribution was moderately but significantly higher upstream of TSSs and downstream of TTSs than within active genes.
claims.source: Thereby, ORC relative read distribution was moderately but significantly higher upstream of TSSs and downstream of TTSs than within active genes (Figure 3a).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claims.claim: The depletion of ORC from gene bodies was statistically significant for approximately 45% of actively transcribed genes.
claims.source: The depletion of ORC from gene bodies was statistically significant for approximately 45% of actively transcribed genes (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: Compared to ORC, Mcm3 and Mcm7 enrichments at TSSs were less prominent, but depletions from gene bodies were more pronounced.
claims.source: Compared to ORC, Mcm3 and Mcm7 enrichments at TSSs were less prominent, but depletions from gene bodies were more pronounced (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), with 75% and 58% of investigated transcribed gene bodies significantly depleted from Mcm3 and Mcm7, respectively (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: 75% of investigated transcribed gene bodies were significantly depleted from Mcm3.
claims.source: Compared to ORC, Mcm3 and Mcm7 enrichments at TSSs were less prominent, but depletions from gene bodies were more pronounced (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), with 75% and 58% of investigated transcribed gene bodies significantly depleted from Mcm3 and Mcm7, respectively (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: 58% of investigated transcribed gene bodies were significantly depleted from Mcm7.
claims.source: Compared to ORC, Mcm3 and Mcm7 enrichments at TSSs were less prominent, but depletions from gene bodies were more pronounced (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), with 75% and 58% of investigated transcribed gene bodies significantly depleted from Mcm3 and Mcm7, respectively (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: Depletion of ORC/MCM from gene bodies was strictly homogeneous from TSS to TTS, strongly suggesting that transcription itself displaces ORC and MCM-DH complexes.
claims.source: Depletion was strictly homogeneous from TSS to TTS, strongly suggesting that transcription itself displaces ORC and MCM-DH complexes (Figure 3a).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the uniform depletion pattern observed across gene bodies.

claims.claim: At silent genes, ORC/MCM were hardly enriched at TSSs and were not depleted from gene bodies.
claims.source: In contrast, at silent genes, ORC/MCM were hardly enriched at TSSs and were not depleted from gene bodies (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: Increasing transcriptional activity did not have any major impact on ORC/MCM enrichments at TSSs.
claims.source: Increasing transcriptional activity (classified as low: 3–10 TPM; mid: 10–40 TPM; high:>40 TPM) did not have any major impact on ORC/MCM enrichments at TSSs (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: ORC/MCM depletion within gene bodies was slightly more pronounced with increasing transcription levels when normalized for input.
claims.source: ORC/MCM depletion within gene bodies was slightly more pronounced with increasing transcription levels when normalized for input (Figure 3d), but this was less convincing without input normalization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: Basal ORC/MCM levels upstream of TSSs and downstream of TTSs were identical.
claims.source: Basal ORC/MCM levels upstream of TSSs and downstream of TTSs were identical, indicating that the local ORC enrichment at TSSs did not result in more MCM loading upstream than downstream of active genes.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of ChIP-seq signals upstream and downstream of genes.

claims.claim: The observation that Mcm3 and Mcm7 are significantly depleted from transcribed gene bodies is consistent with their active displacement by transcription in G1.
claims.source: Our observation that Mcm3 and Mcm7 are significantly depleted from transcribed gene bodies is consistent with their active displacement by transcription in G1, as previously proposed in Drosophila (Powell et al., 2015) and human cells (Macheret and Halazonetis, 2018).
claims.evidence: This interpretation is supported by cited studies in other systems.

claims.claim: The depletion of MCM from transcribed genes contributes to delineating IZs flanked by active genes.
claims.source: This depletion process contributes to delineating IZs flanked by active genes.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MCM depletion from genes creates boundaries for initiation zones.

claims.claim: ORC/MCM density remained constant across non-genic AS borders, suggesting that ORC/MCM are not sufficient to delimit non-genic replication IZs.
claims.source: In contrast, ORC/MCM density remained constant across non-genic AS borders (Figure 2), suggesting that ORC/MCM are not sufficient to delimit non-genic replication IZs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of ORC/MCM enrichment at non-genic AS borders.

claims.claim: In yeast, the number of MCM-DHs loaded at origins correlates with RT.
claims.source: In yeast, it has been reported that the number of MCM-DHs loaded at origins correlates with RT, suggesting how RT profiles can emerge from stochastic origin firing (Das et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited studies in yeast.

claims.claim: In human cells, ORC binding data have been used to predict RT profiles.
claims.source: In human cells, ORC binding data have also been used to predict RT profiles (Miotto et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claims.claim: Expressed genes showed lower ORC/MCM densities than silent genes and intergenic regions.
claims.source: Consistently with Figure 3a, b, expressed genes showed lower ORC/MCM densities than silent genes and intergenic regions (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1d, e).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the 2D histogram analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: The difference in ORC/MCM density between expressed genes and intergenic regions was particularly significant in early- and mid-replicating regions.
claims.source: This was particularly significant in early- and mid-replicating regions, as demonstrated by Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistics (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a, red circles).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claims.claim: The depletion of MCM from expressed genes was more pronounced than for ORC.
claims.source: The depletion was more pronounced for MCM than ORC, as already noted in Figure 3a.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of ORC and MCM ChIP-seq profiles.

claims.claim: The difference between silent genes and intergenic regions in ORC/MCM density was at best marginally significant.
claims.source: In contrast, the difference between silent genes and intergenic regions was at best marginally significant (blue circles).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis.

claims.claim: ORC/MCM densities monotonously decreased from early to late RT windows.
claims.source: In all cases, ORC/MCM densities monotonously decreased from early to late RT windows, but this RT dependency was much attenuated in expressed genes, particularly for MCM, as expected if transcription removes this complex from both early- and late-replicating genes (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the 2D histogram analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: The RT dependency of ORC/MCM density was much attenuated in expressed genes, particularly for MCM.
claims.source: In all cases, ORC/MCM densities monotonously decreased from early to late RT windows, but this RT dependency was much attenuated in expressed genes, particularly for MCM, as expected if transcription removes this complex from both early- and late-replicating genes (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the 2D histogram analysis and is consistent with transcription-mediated removal of MCM.

claims.claim: The analysis did not reveal any clear differences in the levels of ORC/MCM between intergenic ASs, DSs, URRs, and NRRs when bins of similar RT were compared.
claims.source: Strikingly, our analysis did not reveal any clear differences in the levels of ORC/MCM between intergenic ASs, DSs, URRs, and NRRs when bins of similar RT were compared (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistical analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claims.claim: The densities of ORC/MCM across genomic segments were related to RT and gene expression but were not predictive of any RFD pattern.
claims.source: In summary, the densities of ORC/MCM across genomic segments were related to RT and gene expression but were not predictive of any RFD pattern.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comprehensive analysis showing no correlation between ORC/MCM density and RFD patterns after controlling for RT and transcription.

claims.claim: The slope of an RFD segment is proportional to the difference between the density of initiation and termination events within the segment.
claims.source: Strictly speaking, the slope of an RFD segment is proportional to the difference between the density of initiation and termination events within the segment (Audit et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a cited study describing the mathematical relationship.

claims.claim: Initiation events within URRs can almost certainly be excluded.
claims.source: In contrast, we can almost certainly exclude initiation events within URRs, but their ORC/MCM densities were not significantly lower than in ASs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the definition of URRs as unidirectionally replicating regions.

claims.claim: Specific mechanisms repress potential origins in URRs and/or activate them in ASs.
claims.source: This suggests that specific mechanisms repress potential origins in URRs and/or activate them in ASs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that URRs have similar ORC/MCM density to ASs but do not initiate replication.

claims.claim: The density of ORC/MCM is not a reliable predictor of initiation probability, even though ORC density well correlated with RT.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that the density of ORC/MCM is not a reliable predictor of initiation probability, even though ORC density (and to a lesser extent MCM density) well correlated with RT.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comprehensive analysis of ORC/MCM density relative to replication initiation and timing.

claims.claim: Potential origins are widespread through the genome, but additional genetic or epigenetic factors are regulating whether and when they fire.
claims.source: Thus, potential origins are widespread through the genome, but additional genetic or epigenetic factors are regulating whether and when they fire.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ORC/MCM density does not predict initiation sites.

claims.claim: 302 early RTDs covering 642.8 Mb and 287 late RTDs covering 617.4 Mb of the genome were extracted.
claims.source: To confirm this observation, we extracted early and late RTDs employing a threshold of log2(Early/Late) > 1.6 for early RTDs and <−2.0 for late RTDs, which resulted in 302 early RTDs covering 642.8 Mb and 287 late RTDs covering 617.4 Mb of the genome.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of Repli-seq data.

claims.claim: ORC was 1.4 times enriched in early RTDs compared to late RTDs.
claims.source: ORC was 1.4 times enriched in early RTDs compared to late RTDs (Figure 5a, Figure 4—figure supplement 2b, Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figures and table.

claims.claim: Mcm3 and Mcm7 levels showed the same tendencies as ORC but were less contrasted.
claims.source: Mcm3 and Mcm7 levels, although showing the same tendencies, were less contrasted than ORC.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of ChIP-seq signals in early versus late RTDs.

claims.claim: In S-G2-M chromatin, ORC was still significantly enriched in early RTDs, compared to late RTDs, but MCMs were not.
claims.source: In S-G2-M chromatin, ORC was still significantly enriched in early RTDs, compared to late RTDs, but MCMs were not, consistent with completed replication of early but not late RTDs (Figure 5b, Figure 4—figure supplement 2c, Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figures and is consistent with MCM displacement during replication.

claims.claim: The MCM signal is dynamic through the cell cycle.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that the MCM signal is dynamic through the cell cycle as expected.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of G1 and S-G2-M chromatin.

claims.claim: The preferential binding of ORC to early replicating (open) chromatin is not dependent on cell cycle stage.
claims.source: These results also show that the preferential binding of ORC to early replicating (open) chromatin is not dependent on cell cycle stage.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the persistence of ORC enrichment in early RTDs in S-G2-M chromatin.

claims.claim: Orc1 in human cells is degraded at the G1-S transition and in early S phase.
claims.source: Given that Orc1 in human cells is degraded at the G1-S transition and in early S phase (Kreitz et al., 2001; Méndez et al., 2002; Ohta et al., 2003), it might appear surprising that we detect Orc2 and Orc3 binding to S-G2-M chromatin.
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claims.claim: Orc1 reappears as cells enter mitosis and is the first ORC subunit to bind to mitotic chromosomes, but other ORC subunits seem to join only in daughter G1 cells.
claims.source: In human cells, Orc1 reappears as cells enter mitosis and is the first ORC subunit to bind to mitotic chromosomes, but other ORC subunits seem to join only in daughter G1 cells (Kara et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claims.claim: GFP‐tagged Orc1 was found to associate with chromatin throughout mitosis in living Chinese hamster cells and to co-localize with Orc4 in metaphase spreads.
claims.source: Nevertheless, GFP‐tagged Orc1 was found to associate with chromatin throughout mitosis in living Chinese hamster cells and to co-localize with Orc4 in metaphase spreads (Okuno et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claims.claim: The binding of Orc2 and Orc3 detected in S-G2-M may either occur independently of Orc1 or reflect the binding of the entire complex in late mitotic cells.
claims.source: The binding of Orc2 and Orc3 we detect in S-G2-M may either occur independently of Orc1 or reflect the binding of the entire complex in late mitotic cells.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of ORC binding in S-G2-M.

claims.claim: H4K20me3 is involved in licensing a subset of late-replicating regions.
claims.source: We and others recently demonstrated that H4K20me3 is involved in licensing a subset of late-replicating regions (Benetti et al., 2007; Brustel et al., 2017; Pannetier et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited studies including work from the authors' group.

claims.claim: ORC and, to a lower extent, MCM were enriched at H4K20me3 peaks.
claims.source: We calculated ORC/MCM relative read frequencies binned at 1 kb resolution at H4K20me3/H4K20me1 peaks > 1 kb (12,251 and 6277 peaks, respectively). ORC and, to a lower extent, MCM were enriched at H4K20me3, but not H4K20me1 peaks (Figure 5c, Figure 5—figure supplement 1e).

results.result: ChIP validation using EBV oriP as a positive control demonstrates successful enrichment of ORC and MCM at the dyad symmetry element in G1 cells, with expected reduction of MCM in S-G2-M cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C40 provide qPCR validation of ChIP quality using the well-characterized EBV oriP origin. The data show expected enrichment patterns and cell cycle dynamics, validating the technical approach. This is a standard quality control for ChIP experiments.

results.result: ChIP-seq of ORC subunits (Orc2, Orc3) and MCM proteins (Mcm3, Mcm7) in G1-enriched Raji cells produces reproducible signals with high Pearson correlation coefficients (r=0.866 for Orc2/Orc3, r=0.879 for Mcm3/Mcm7).
results.evaluation: Claims C41, C44, and C45 demonstrate technical reproducibility of the ChIP-seq experiments through high correlation between biological replicates. The correlation coefficients are appropriately high (>0.85) for ChIP-seq replicates, supporting data quality.

results.result: ORC ChIP-seq data shows enrichment at DNase hypersensitive sites and agreement with previously published K562 Orc2 ChIP-seq data, validating the experimental approach.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C48 provide multiple lines of validation: comparison with published data (C46-C47), enrichment at expected genomic features (DNase HS sites, C48), and acknowledgment of input bias (C42-C43). These validations support the reliability of the ChIP-seq data.

results.result: ORC and MCM are significantly and homogeneously depleted from transcribed gene bodies, with MCM showing more pronounced depletion (75% and 58% of genes significantly depleted for Mcm3 and Mcm7, respectively) than ORC (45% of genes). Both are enriched at active TSSs, with depletion being uniform across gene bodies and independent of transcription level.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C65-C76 collectively demonstrate transcription-dependent depletion of ORC/MCM from gene bodies using ChIP-seq data with appropriate statistical analysis. The uniform depletion pattern (C71) and lack of depletion at silent genes (C72) support the interpretation that active transcription displaces these complexes. The data are internally consistent and supported by cited studies in other organisms (C76).

results.result: ORC is enriched at gene promoters, but MCMs show less enrichment at TSSs than ORC, and MCM levels are similar upstream and downstream of genes, indicating that ORC enrichment at TSSs does not result in preferential MCM loading upstream of genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C127, and C128 demonstrate differential enrichment patterns between ORC and MCM at promoters. The observation that MCM levels are equivalent upstream and downstream of genes (C75, C128) despite ORC enrichment at TSSs is well-supported by the ChIP-seq data and argues against preferential licensing at promoters.

results.result: OK-seq analysis identified 2957 ascending segments (ASs) representing initiation zones, classified into three types based on proximity to transcribed genes: type 1 (22.8%, flanked by active genes on both sides), type 2 (34.7%, one border with active gene), and non-genic (17.1%). Type 1 and 2 ASs are predominantly early-replicating, while non-genic ASs are late-replicating.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C55 describe the classification of initiation zones based on OK-seq data combined with RNA-seq. The classification scheme is logical and the replication timing patterns (C55) are consistent with previous observations. The data provide a framework for analyzing ORC/MCM distribution relative to different IZ types.

results.result: ORC and MCM are enriched within ASs compared to flanking regions, with enrichment being dependent on transcriptional activity at AS borders. Type 1 and 2 ASs show increased ORC/MCM at borders associated with active genes, while no enrichment is detected within non-genic ASs.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C60, C62 demonstrate that ORC/MCM enrichment at initiation zones is context-dependent, being most prominent when ASs are flanked by active transcription. The lack of enrichment in non-genic ASs (C59) is a key observation suggesting that ORC/MCM density alone does not define all initiation zones. The data are clearly presented in Figure 2.

results.result: ORC and MCM are more abundant in early- than in late-replicating domains, with ORC showing stronger correlation with replication timing than MCM. Expressed genes show lower ORC/MCM densities than silent genes and intergenic regions, particularly in early- and mid-replicating regions, with MCM depletion being more pronounced than ORC.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C81-C86 demonstrate the relationship between ORC/MCM density and replication timing using 2D histogram analysis. The statistical analysis (Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests, C82) supports the significance of differences. The attenuation of RT dependency in expressed genes (C86) is consistent with transcription-mediated removal of MCM.

results.result: After controlling for replication timing and transcription, no significant differences in ORC/MCM density are detected between initiation zones (ASs), termination zones (DSs), unidirectionally replicating regions (URRs), and randomly replicating regions (NRRs). This indicates that ORC/MCM density does not solely regulate initiation probability, and additional factors must specify where replication initiates.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C87-C93 present the central finding that ORC/MCM density does not predict replication fork directionality patterns when RT and transcription are controlled. The statistical analysis (C87) and the observation that URRs have similar ORC/MCM density to ASs despite lacking initiation (C90-C91) strongly support this conclusion. This is a major conceptual advance challenging simple models of origin specification.

results.result: ORC density correlates well with replication timing, but MCM density shows weaker correlation with RT and lacks correlation with RFD slope, suggesting that origin-firing probability is not solely regulated by MCM-DH density.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C146-C149 demonstrate differential correlations between ORC and MCM density with replication parameters. The observation that MCM density does not correlate with RFD slope (C148) despite ORC correlation with RT (C146) is well-supported by the 2D histogram analyses in Figure 4 and is critical for the interpretation that licensing density alone does not determine initiation sites.

results.result: In G1 chromatin, ORC is 1.4-fold enriched in early versus late RTDs, with MCM showing similar but less pronounced enrichment. In S-G2-M chromatin, ORC remains enriched in early RTDs while MCM enrichment is lost, demonstrating cell cycle dynamics of MCM and cell cycle-independent ORC binding to early-replicating chromatin.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C99 demonstrate cell cycle dynamics of ORC and MCM binding using chromatin from different cell cycle stages. The loss of MCM enrichment in S-G2-M (C97) is consistent with MCM displacement during replication and validates the biological relevance of the findings. The persistence of ORC enrichment (C99) provides insight into ORC binding mechanisms.

results.result: H4K20me3 is enriched in late-replicating non-genic initiation zones, and ORC/MCM are enriched at H4K20me3-high non-genic ASs compared to H4K20me3-low ASs, suggesting that H4K20me3 contributes to specifying these regions as master initiation zones in late-replicating DNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C105-C109 link H4K20me3 to origin licensing in a specific subset of late-replicating initiation zones. The enrichment of ORC/MCM at H4K20me3-high non-genic ASs (C107) and the cell cycle dynamics (C109) support this connection. This identifies the first histone modification specific for late-replicating non-genic ASs (C106).

results.result: H4K20me3 shows a broader distribution in NRRs compared to other genomic regions, with high densities detected in late-replicating gene deserts of null RFD. ORC/MCM are more abundant at H4K20me3-high than H4K20me3-low bins in NRRs, supporting the hypothesis that H4K20me3 facilitates origin licensing in heterochromatic segments.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C117 extend the H4K20me3 analysis to randomly replicating regions (NRRs). The observation that NRRs show a specific, broader distribution of H4K20me3 (C114) and that ORC/MCM are enriched at H4K20me3-high bins in NRRs (C116) provides additional support for the role of H4K20me3 in origin licensing in heterochromatin. The data are consistent with previous findings (C117, C141).

results.result: Analysis of mouse ESC OK-seq data shows that early replication control elements (ERCEs) identified by Sima et al. fall within initiation zones, and the aggregate of 1835 predicted ERCEs shows a significant positive RFD shift indicative of efficient replication initiation, confirmed in mouse primary B cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C160 provide independent validation of the relationship between open chromatin marks and initiation zones using published ERCE data. The positive RFD shift at ERCEs (C159) and confirmation in a different cell type (C160) support the generality of the findings. This analysis strengthens the connection between chromatin features and origin specification.

results.result: The findings support a cascade model for replication initiation in which most of the genome (except transcribed genes) is licensed for replication, but additional factors like transcription and epigenetic marks specify master zones of higher initiation efficiency, with the distributed licensing pattern allowing stochastic activation of secondary origins.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C120, C161-C162, C164-C166, C168 synthesize the major findings into a coherent model. The widespread distribution of ORC/MCM (C118, C164) combined with the lack of correlation between density and initiation sites (C161-C162) supports the cascade model. The model is consistent with all the presented data and provides a framework for understanding mammalian replication initiation.

results.result: Transcription has dual effects on origin activity: active transcription removes ORC/MCM from gene bodies (reducing initiation capacity), while ORC enrichment at TSSs may facilitate licensing. MCM depletion from transcribed genes contributes to delineating IZs flanked by active genes, but ORC/MCM are not sufficient to delimit non-genic IZs.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C122, C77-C78 integrate the observations about transcription effects into a coherent interpretation. The dual positive and negative effects (C121) are well-supported by the data showing depletion from gene bodies and enrichment at TSSs. The inference that depletion contributes to IZ delineation (C77) is logical, and the observation that this mechanism doesn't apply to non-genic IZs (C78) highlights the complexity of origin specification.

results.result: Multiple open chromatin marks at IZs (H2A.Z, H3K4me1, H3K27ac, DNase HS) may promote both origin licensing and firing through mechanisms involving H2A.Z recruitment of SUV420H1 (leading to H4K20me2 and ORC1 interaction), nucleosome-free gaps, and Treslin/MTBP binding sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C137 synthesize literature findings about chromatin marks at IZs and their potential mechanisms. While largely based on cited studies (C129, C131-C136), the integration with the current findings (C137) is logical. However, these are largely mechanistic speculations based on correlations and literature, not directly tested in this study.

results.result: Replication licensing is functionally linked to H4K20me3 in a specific subset of late-replicating domains, as demonstrated by elevated ORC and MCM levels at H4K20me3-enriched non-genic ASs and NRRs.
results.evaluation: Claims C142, C141, C104, C23 establish the functional link between H4K20me3 and origin licensing in late-replicating regions. The current data (C142) build on previous work from the authors' group (C141, C23, C104) and provide genome-wide support for this connection. The enrichment of ORC/MCM at H4K20me3-high regions is well-documented in Figures 5f and 6b.

results.result: While models propose that RT results from the spatial distribution of potential origins (derived from ORC/MCM density or epigenetic marks), the current data suggest that open chromatin independently facilitates both ORC binding in G1 and firing factor access in S phase, and that only MCM-DHs associated with appropriate chromatin marks are causative of RT.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C153 discuss models for RT determination and their relationship to the current findings. While the reasoning is logical (C151-C152), the conclusion that only MCM-DHs with appropriate chromatin marks determine RT (C153) is speculative and not directly tested. The claims appropriately acknowledge this uncertainty ('Probably', C153), but additional experiments would be needed to definitively establish causality.

results.result: Despite Orc1 degradation at G1-S transition, Orc2 and Orc3 are detected in S-G2-M chromatin, which may occur independently of Orc1 or reflect binding of the entire complex in late mitotic cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C103 address an apparent paradox in the data. While the detection of Orc2/Orc3 in S-G2-M is supported by the ChIP-seq data, the mechanistic explanation (C103) is speculative. The cited literature (C100-C102) provides context but doesn't resolve the uncertainty. This observation warrants further investigation but doesn't undermine the main conclusions.

results.result: Open chromatin structures at Ma-IZs and ERCEs might facilitate both origin licensing in G1 and firing factor binding in S phase, with links between chromatin structure, transcription, and origin regulation facilitating timely origin activation during development.
results.evaluation: Claims C163, C167, C169-C170 propose mechanistic models for how chromatin structure regulates origin specification and timing. While consistent with the data and supported by cited studies (C163), these are largely speculative interpretations about mechanisms not directly tested in this study. The dual role of open chromatin (C167) is a reasonable hypothesis but requires experimental validation.
